title: Canadian Business Registration
subtitle: Know which forms belong to your business before you start filing.

blocks.text: You have picked a business idea, but three websites each offer a “register” button. Which one gets you ready to work? Government websites can make a small business feel like it needs its own filing cabinet before it has its first customer.
Make the forms make sense.
blocks.detail: A clear registration map helps you spend time and fees only on the steps your business needs.
blocks.extra: Section 03 explains each layer, from your name to your permits.

sections.title: Start with a map of your business

blocks.text: Registration has several layers. A registry records a business name or creates a corporation. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) handles tax accounts. Other offices handle licences and permits. Finishing one layer does not finish the others.

Start by writing down your business structure, where you will work, the name you will use and the work you will do. A home organizing service raises different questions from a restaurant or a building company. Use those facts to find the right official pages before you pay any fee.
The registry layer

A sole proprietor may need to register a business name with the province or territory. Incorporating is a different filing that creates a corporation. The Canadian Intellectual Property Office also points out that a business name is not a trademark. Registering your name does not register a trademark.
Before you order signs, search the business registry and check for similar trademarks. A name search is useful homework, but it does not promise your name is free of legal conflicts.
The CRA layer

The CRA uses a nine-digit business number, or BN, to identify a business. GST/HST and payroll are separate tax accounts linked to that number. The CRA says some provincial registrations give you a BN, but having one does not mean every tax account is open.

Check which accounts your work needs, instead of asking for every option. If you plan to hire, set up payroll before you pay anyone. You still report your income even if your unincorporated business does not need a BN. Registering is not the test for whether your earnings count.
Label each number when you save it. A provincial registry number and a CRA BN do different jobs, even when they arrive during the same setup.
The permission layer

BizPaL is a free government tool that finds permits and licences. Search by your location and your activities, then confirm the results with the office that issues each permit. The search helps you find what you need, but it does not give you permission to operate.

items.title: “My business name receipt is a Canada-wide business licence.”
items.text: Your name registration, your tax accounts, local permits and any industry licence each answer a different question. Check each layer that fits your work.

blocks.text: The sales tax layer

items.title: GST/HST
items.text: Collected through the CRA everywhere in Canada. In Ontario and the Atlantic provinces, the single HST covers both the federal and provincial parts.

items.title: BRITISH COLUMBIA, SASKATCHEWAN, MANITOBA
items.text: Each runs its own provincial sales tax with its own registration and limits. Check the province’s site, separate from the CRA.

items.title: QUEBEC
items.text: Revenu Québec runs the QST and, for most Quebec businesses, the GST too.

items.title: ALBERTA AND THE TERRITORIES
items.text: No provincial sales tax, but the GST rules still apply.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: Sandra’s missing folder

blocks.text: Sandra’s missing folder
paragraphs: Sandra lived in London, Ontario. She wanted to start a home organizing service while keeping her part-time job. She had labelled sample storage bins and set money aside for flyers. Her launch folder held a logo and a flyer, but no plan for registering.

A neighbour asked whether her invoices would say Sandra or Clear Space Home Organizing. Sandra opened a business website and almost chose to incorporate, because it sounded the most complete. Then another page mentioned a business number. Did both buttons do the same thing?

She paused the flyer order. First she wrote down the business she meant to run: one owner, an Ontario business name and organizing work in clients’ homes. She stayed a sole proprietor and checked Ontario’s name rule. She also made separate notes for CRA accounts and local permits.

She registered the name and saved the receipt with a clear label. She did not write “all done” across the folder. Her permit search raised questions about running an office from home. She asked the city about her actual work and kept the reply next to her search results.

Before the flyers went to print, a customer asked if Sandra could also haul away renovation waste. She had not planned that service, so she said no while she checked what it would change. Her launch was smaller than the flyer draft, but its scope was clear. The first bin she labelled for her own office said “Registration records.”

blocks.text: Sandra’s story is a made-up example, not a promised approval timeline. Her useful habit was keeping proof beside each finished step and leaving open questions in plain sight.
Keep your next step visible.
blocks.detail: Separate records let you answer a new business question in minutes, without starting your research over.
blocks.extra: Section 05 shows you how to build that file for your own business.

blocks.text: Try this walkthrough for Sandra’s service. Use four labelled sections in a folder, and mark each item “confirmed,” “to file” or “needs an answer.” These are your own planning labels, not official statuses.

items.title: Business facts: write down the structure, the Ontario location, the business name and the home organizing work. Note whether you will sell goods or hire staff.

Registry: Ontario’s Business Names Act says a person using a name other than their own must register it. Register through the Ontario Business Registry. It costs $60 and lasts five years, so note the renewal date. Save the details you sent and the receipt.
CRA: check whether you already have a BN before you ask for one. Review the accounts your work needs, and save the confirmation for each account you open.
Permits: run a BizPaL search for your location and work. Ask the city about your home office and services. Save the answers and any approvals in their own section.

blocks.text: The rules on using your own name vary. B.C. says a sole proprietor working under their personal name does not need name approval or registration. Quebec generally requires registration when the name does not include the owner’s first and last names. Tobacco shops and tanning salons there must register no matter what.

The CRA’s small supplier test looks at taxable sales before expenses, worldwide, including those of associated businesses. You must register once you pass $30,000 in one calendar quarter or over four quarters in a row. It tests sales, not profit. Some work, such as taxi and ride-sharing services, must register from the first dollar.
Check provincial sales tax where it applies. Adding product sales to a service can raise questions your first plan did not cover.

items.title: “Federal incorporation removes provincial registration checks.”
items.text: Corporations Canada says federal companies must register in each province where they do business. Each province has its own rules.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Set a review reminder whenever your location, name or work changes, plus one for your name renewal date. Keep official confirmations together and protect your logins. A folder called “Receipts somewhere” is not a filing system anyone deserves.
Quick Check

items.title: Does registering a trade name turn a sole proprietorship into a corporation?
Does a BizPaL result approve your permit application?
items.text: Confirm requirements and apply with the issuing authority.

items.title: Is the usual GST/HST small supplier test based on profit after expenses?
items.text: It uses taxable sales before expenses, with rules about what to include.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Sandra receives a name registration receipt. What should she do next? A. Assume all permissions are complete. · B. Check remaining tax and permit layers. · C. Call her business a corporation.
items.text: The receipt records the name filing; remaining requirements need separate checks.

items.title: A B.C. sole proprietor works under her personal name. What is the sound approach? A. Use Ontario’s rule. · B. Assume there are no tax obligations. · C. Check B.C.’s own-name exception and other applicable layers.
items.text: B.C.’s registry exception does not answer every tax or permit question.

items.title: A business already has a CRA BN and now needs a payroll account. What should it check? A. How to add the required account to its existing BN. · B. How to buy another operating name. · C. Whether its logo includes nine digits.
items.text: CRA program accounts connect to the business’s existing BN.

items.title: Write one unresolved registration question for a proposed business, and name the authority you would ask.
items.text: Does my home office need permission for customer visits? Ask the municipality about the actual activity.

blocks.text: Match the filing to the question. A name record, CRA account and permission to carry out an activity each need their own evidence.
Use your own business idea or practise with Sandra’s service. Give enough detail to choose an official next step, but leave sensitive numbers off this sheet.
Make your four-section evidence file and add one official source to it. Mark the first open question and check it by the date you set below.

items.title: Trade name
items.text: The name a business uses in public.

items.title: Incorporation
items.text: The process that creates a corporation.

items.title: Business number
items.text: The CRA’s nine-digit number for a business.

items.title: Program account
items.text: An account for one tax program, such as GST/HST or payroll.

items.title: Permit
items.text: Permission for a specific activity or use.

items.title: Trademark
items.text: A sign that sets your goods or services apart from others.
